questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 1 asks which levels biodiversity includes beyond species counts.

options.text: Only species richness in a habitat
Only genetic variation within one species
Only ecosystem types on a continent

questions.explanation: Biodiversity spans genetic, species and ecosystem levels. Counting only species misses the other two levels.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Place a producer in a food chain
questions.stem: Translator's note 2 asks which organism occupies the first trophic level in a grassland chain.
questions.explanation: Producers occupy the first trophic level by converting energy into biomass. Consumers and decomposers feed on that biomass.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 3 asks which event begins primary succession on bare rock.

options.text: A forest fire in an established woodland
A flood that kills some plants
A volcanic lava flow creating new rock

questions.explanation: Primary succession starts on substrates without soil, such as new volcanic rock. Secondary succession follows disturbance where soil remains.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 4 describes bees gaining nectar while flowers gain pollination; what interaction is this?
questions.explanation: Both partners gain from the interaction, which defines mutualism. Commensalism, parasitism and competition describe different outcomes.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 5 asks which niche is limited by competitors and predators.
questions.explanation: The realised niche is the portion of the fundamental niche actually occupied once biotic interactions are considered.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 6 describes fishing faster than stocks can recover; what term fits?
questions.explanation: Harvesting beyond the rate of renewal depletes the stock, which is overexploitation. Sustainable yield stays within renewal.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 7 asks which consequence follows from splitting a forest into small patches.

options.text: Increased edge habitat and smaller cores

questions.explanation: Fragmentation increases edge relative to core area and reduces connectivity. It does not enlarge core habitat or boost diversity.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a point source of pollution
questions.stem: Translator's note 8 asks which discharge is a point source.

options.text: A pipe from a treatment plant

questions.explanation: A point source enters at a single identifiable location, such as a pipe. Diffuse runoff is nonpoint.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 9 removes top predators from a lake; what likely happens to algae?
questions.explanation: Removing predators releases grazers, which consume more algae, so algae decreases. The cascade runs through the intermediate level.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 10 asks why diverse communities often resist disturbance better.

options.text: Because one species does all the work
Because multiple species can fill roles

questions.explanation: Higher diversity provides functional redundancy, so if one species declines another can maintain the role. That supports stability.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain biomagnification up a food chain
questions.stem: Translator's note 11 asks why a persistent toxin reaches high levels in top predators.

options.text: Because water flushes the toxin upward
Because toxin concentrates at each level

questions.explanation: Persistent toxins are retained and concentrated as they pass up the food chain, so top predators carry the highest levels.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 12 asks why an experiment needs more than one replicate per treatment.

options.text: To estimate variability and improve inference
To guarantee the hypothesis is true
To reduce the number of treatments

questions.explanation: Replication provides an estimate of natural variability, which is needed for statistical inference. It does not prove hypotheses or remove confounders.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE

stimulus.body: Site X has 10 species with one dominant species making 90 percent of individuals. Site Y has 10 species with roughly equal abundances. Both have the same species richness.

questions.stem: Translator's note 13 asks which site has higher evenness.

options.text: Site X, because one species dominates
Site Y, because abundances are balanced

questions.explanation: Evenness measures how equally individuals are distributed among species. Site Y is more even because no species dominates.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 14 asks why only about 10 percent of energy transfers between trophic levels.

options.text: Because energy is created at each level
Because most energy is lost as heat and metabolism

questions.explanation: Most energy is used for metabolism, movement and heat, leaving only a fraction for growth and reproduction. That limits transfer efficiency.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 15 asks which species likely appears first on bare volcanic rock.
questions.explanation: Pioneer species such as lichens tolerate extreme conditions and begin soil formation. Later species require that improved substrate.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 16 asks what happens when two species compete for the same limited resource.

options.text: One may exclude the other or partition the resource

questions.explanation: Competition can lead to exclusion or to resource partitioning that allows coexistence. It does not automatically create mutualism or new resources.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 17 asks what the competitive exclusion principle predicts for two identical niches.

options.text: One will eventually exclude the other

questions.explanation: If two species occupy identical niches, competition drives one to exclude the other. Coexistence requires niche differentiation.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE

stimulus.body: A fish stock grows by 200 individuals per year. Harvest is 250 individuals per year. The stock has declined for three consecutive years.

questions.stem: Translator's note 18 asks what the data imply about harvest.
questions.explanation: Harvest above growth depletes the stock, as shown by the decline. Sustainable harvest cannot exceed 200 individuals per year.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 19 asks what an edge effect means for forest interior species.

options.text: Interior species face altered conditions near edges

questions.explanation: Edges change light, temperature and humidity, affecting interior species. The effect is not limited to predators.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 20 asks which sequence follows excess nutrient input to a lake.
questions.explanation: Excess nutrients stimulate algal growth; when algae die, decomposition consumes oxygen. The sequence is nutrient, bloom, depletion.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 21 removes a mesopredator from a three-level chain; what is likely?

options.text: Prey decreases and basal resource increases
Prey increases and basal resource decreases

questions.explanation: Without the mesopredator, prey is released and consumes more of the basal resource, which declines. The effect propagates downward.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 22 asks which term means returning to the original state after disturbance.
questions.explanation: Resilience is the ability to recover after disturbance. Resistance is the ability to withstand it without changing.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify which organisms face highest risk
questions.stem: Translator's note 23 asks which organisms face the greatest biomagnification risk.
questions.explanation: Top predators accumulate the highest concentrations because toxins biomagnify at each trophic transfer.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 24 asks what makes an experiment controlled.

options.text: It uses the largest sample size
It runs for a long time
It compares treated and untreated groups

questions.explanation: A controlled experiment compares groups that differ in the treatment while other conditions are held constant. Size, measurement and duration are separate issues.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why biodiversity matters for services
questions.stem: Translator's note 25 asks why losing species can reduce ecosystem services.

answer.exemplar: Species contribute to processes such as pollination and nutrient cycling, so losing species can weaken or remove services that humans depend on.

questions.explanation: Biodiversity underpins ecosystem functions and services. Species loss can reduce resilience and eliminate functions with no substitute.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 26 asks which sequence forms a valid food chain.
questions.explanation: Energy flows from producer to herbivore to carnivore. Reversing the order or skipping levels breaks the chain.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 27 asks what a climax community represents in classical succession.

options.text: The first colonisers on bare rock

questions.explanation: In classical succession, the climax community is the relatively stable assemblage that persists under the regional climate. Modern views allow multiple stable states.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 28 describes barnacles on a whale gaining transport while the whale is unaffected; what interaction is this?
questions.explanation: Only the barnacle benefits while the whale is unaffected, which defines commensalism.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 29 asks how similar species coexist in the same habitat.
questions.explanation: Niche partitioning reduces overlap in resource use, allowing coexistence. Identical resource use would lead to competitive exclusion.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 30 asks what maximum sustainable yield represents.

options.text: The largest possible catch ever recorded
The harvest that empties the stock
The largest harvest that can be sustained indefinitely

questions.explanation: Maximum sustainable yield is the largest harvest rate that does not deplete the stock over time. Larger catches deplete the resource.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 31 asks why conservation corridors are created between fragments.

options.text: To allow movement and gene flow

questions.explanation: Corridors connect fragments, allowing organisms to move and maintain gene flow. They are not meant to remove predators or shrink habitat.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 32 asks what high biological oxygen demand indicates.
questions.explanation: High BOD means microbes consume much oxygen decomposing organic matter, indicating organic pollution. It does not mean high dissolved oxygen.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Predict effects of top predator recovery
questions.stem: Translator's note 33 reintroduces top predators to a degraded lake; what is likely?

options.text: Grazers decrease and algae decreases? wait

questions.explanation: Reintroducing predators reduces grazers, which releases algae to increase. The cascade propagates downward with alternating signs.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 34 asks what the insurance hypothesis says about diversity.

options.text: Diverse communities buffer function against species loss

questions.explanation: The insurance hypothesis states that diversity provides a buffer, so ecosystem function persists even if some species are lost.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 35 asks why fat-soluble toxins biomagnify more than water-soluble ones.

options.text: Because they are stored in tissues and retained

questions.explanation: Fat-soluble toxins are stored in tissues and not easily excreted, so they accumulate and magnify up the food chain.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 36 asks how to design a control for a fertiliser experiment.

answer.exemplar: Keep all conditions identical except fertiliser, with untreated plots receiving no fertiliser but the same water, light and handling.

questions.explanation: A valid control differs only in the treatment. Matching other conditions isolates the fertiliser effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 37 asks what species richness counts.
questions.explanation: Species richness is simply the number of species in a community. Abundance, biomass and genetic variation are different measures.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 38 asks which organism is a secondary consumer.
questions.explanation: A secondary consumer eats primary consumers. The fox eating a rabbit fits, while grass is a producer and rabbit is a primary consumer.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 39 asks what facilitation means in succession.

options.text: Early species improve conditions for later ones

questions.explanation: Facilitation occurs when early colonisers improve conditions, making establishment easier for later species.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 40 describes a tick feeding on a dog, harming the dog; what interaction is this?

options.text: Parasitism, one benefits and one is harmed

questions.explanation: One organism benefits at the expense of the other, which defines parasitism. Mutualism and commensalism lack harm.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 41 asks which factor is part of a species' niche.
questions.explanation: A niche includes the species' role, resource use and environmental tolerances. Habitat and population size are related but not the whole niche.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a tragedy of the commons
questions.stem: Translator's note 42 describes herders adding animals to a shared pasture until it degrades; what concept is this?
questions.explanation: Shared resources can be overused when individuals act in their own interest, degrading the commons. That is the tragedy of the commons.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 43 asks what minimum viable population means.

options.text: The smallest population likely to persist
The population in one habitat patch

questions.explanation: Minimum viable population is the smallest size with a high probability of persisting. Below it, extinction risk rises.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 44 asks which input is a nonpoint source.

options.text: A discharge from a treatment plant

questions.explanation: Nonpoint sources are diffuse and lack a single entry point, such as agricultural runoff. Pipes and outfalls are point sources.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 45 asks what a trophic cascade is.

options.text: A stable population with no change
A food chain with one level
Indirect effects that propagate across levels

questions.explanation: A trophic cascade is an indirect effect that propagates through multiple levels of a food web. It is more than a single link.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 46 asks why diversity can stabilise ecosystem function.

options.text: Because species respond differently to fluctuations

questions.explanation: Different species respond differently to environmental fluctuations, so their combined function is more stable. This is the portfolio effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why producers have lowest toxin levels
questions.stem: Translator's note 47 asks why producers have the lowest toxin concentrations.

options.text: Because they create toxins from nothing
Because they excrete all toxins instantly
Because they are at the base of the chain
Because predators dilute toxins for them

questions.explanation: Producers are at the base and have not accumulated toxins through consumption, so their concentrations are lowest.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 48 asks what pseudoreplication means.
questions.explanation: Pseudoreplication occurs when samples that are not independent are treated as independent replicates, inflating apparent replication.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 49 asks what defines a biodiversity hotspot.

options.text: An area with no human impact

questions.explanation: A hotspot requires high endemism and significant habitat loss. High species richness alone is not enough.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why food chains are short
questions.stem: Translator's note 50 asks why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels.

options.text: Because energy increases at each level
Because energy loss limits higher levels

questions.explanation: Energy loss at each transfer leaves too little energy to support additional levels, limiting chain length.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 51 asks what inhibition means in succession.
questions.explanation: Inhibition occurs when early colonisers make conditions less suitable for later species, slowing or blocking their establishment.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 52 describes a large tree shading out small plants without being affected; what interaction is this?
questions.explanation: One organism is harmed while the other is unaffected, which defines amensalism. The tree is unaffected and the shaded plants suffer.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 53 asks how warblers in the same tree coexist.

options.text: By using different parts of the tree

questions.explanation: Using different parts of the tree partitions the resource and reduces competition, allowing coexistence.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 54 asks why open-access fisheries tend to be overharvested.

answer.exemplar: When no one owns the resource, each harvester gains the full benefit but shares the cost, encouraging overuse until the stock declines.

questions.explanation: Open access creates an incentive to harvest before others do, leading to overuse. Regulation or property rights can prevent depletion.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 55 asks what island biogeography predicts for species richness.

options.text: Larger and nearer islands have more species
Smaller and farther islands have more species

questions.explanation: Species richness increases with island area and decreases with distance from the mainland. Both factors matter.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 56 asks what thermal pollution does to dissolved oxygen.
questions.explanation: Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, so thermal pollution reduces oxygen available to aquatic organisms.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 57 increases herbivores in a grassland; what happens to producers?
questions.explanation: More herbivores consume more plant biomass, so producers decrease. The effect is direct, not a multi-level cascade.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 58 asks what functional redundancy means.

options.text: Multiple species can perform the same function

questions.explanation: Functional redundancy means several species can perform the same ecological function, buffering against species loss.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 59 asks which pollutant is known for biomagnification.
questions.explanation: Persistent fat-soluble toxins such as DDT and mercury biomagnify because they are retained in tissues and concentrated up the chain.

provenance.author: bank-team-environmental-science
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.stem: Translator's note 60 asks how to state a testable hypothesis for a fertiliser effect.

answer.exemplar: If nitrogen fertiliser is added, then plant biomass will increase compared with unfertilised plots, assuming other conditions are equal.

questions.explanation: A testable hypothesis links the manipulation to a measurable prediction under controlled conditions. Vague claims are not testable.
